claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy contains fine, uniformly distributed compositional elements.
The as-built alloy contains small strengthening precipitates.
At about 750 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere, Cr selectively oxidizes at grain boundaries.
Ti may make a minor contribution to grain-boundary oxidation.
Selective oxidation forms thin, discontinuous oxide films at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary oxidation produces local compositional depletion zones.
Discontinuous grain-boundary oxides act as stress concentrators that nucleate and propagate microcracks.
Oxidation-induced microcracking degrades mechanical performance, especially fatigue strength.
Significant oxide layers do not form under reducing conditions.
Prolonged exposure under reducing conditions may coarsen the alloy's initial nanoscale precipitates.
Precipitate coarsening reduces strengthening and causes modest mechanical degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will increase Cr-rich grain-boundary oxide formation relative to the as-built state.
Oxidizing exposure will increase microcrack density relative to the as-built state.
Oxidizing exposure will cause a larger loss of fatigue life and yield strength than reducing exposure.
Reducing exposure will cause minimal oxidation and less mechanical degradation than oxidizing exposure.
Aging near 750 °C is relevant to temporal evolution of the matrix and gamma-prime precipitates in this Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti alloy system.
The proposed oxidation-versus-coarsening mechanism remains valid for exposures up to 50 hours.
Intermediate gas compositions, other temperatures, or longer durations may produce mixed or alternative degradation mechanisms.
Comparing otherwise identical samples exposed at 750 °C for 10, 25, and 50 hours in oxidizing and low-oxygen atmospheres is the proposed controlled test.

contradictions.description: The design treats forming gas and inert gas as interchangeable examples of a reducing atmosphere. An inert atmosphere is low in oxygen but is not necessarily chemically reducing, so these conditions may impose different oxygen potentials.

The hypothesis says oxide layers do not form in reducing environments, whereas the mechanism and prediction allow an absence of significant oxidation or minimal oxide formation. These differ between complete absence and a small nonzero amount.
